meta.blurb: Why do some countries have so much and others so little? Follow the long story from the first farms to the first factories, and weigh the answers that historians offer: place, rules and sheer chance.
meta.bible: A single narrator speaks to the reader, curious, fair and clear. Places: Fertile Crescent, Mesopotamia, Uruk (an early city), Levant, Eurasia, Yangtze (river in China), Mexico, Andes, Americas, Africa, New Guinea, Mediterranean, Europe, China, India, Baghdad, Cairo, Kaifeng, Egypt, Britain, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore, Switzerland, Germany, Belgium, France, Spain, Portugal, Caribbean, Atlantic. People (all long dead): Christopher Columbus sailed for Spain in 1492; Vasco da Gama of Portugal reached India in 1498; Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press in Germany about 1450; Thomas Newcomen built a steam pumping engine in 1712; James Watt improved it in the 1760s; Edward Jenner showed vaccination in 1796. Events: the Black Death reached Europe in 1347; the Great Divergence is the widening gap in wealth after about 1800; the Meiji government of Japan began in 1868; the Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the 1700s; the first public steam railway opened in 1825. Key terms: Surplus, Teosinte, Sorghum, Taro, Millet, Barley, Granaries, Scribes, Bronze, Plough, Ploughs, Lorries, Ironmonger, Serfs, Locomotives, Smallpox, Measles, Influenza, Cowpox, Vaccine, Vaccination, Malaria, Landlocked, Institutions, Divergence, Colonised, Cobs, Ore, Tin, Copper, Duchies, Clique, Tinkering. Voice and tone: curious, balanced and honest about what is still debated; no invented numbers or quotes; slavery and disease treated factually and without gore; never any suggestion that some peoples are less able than others.

B1B2: Look at the world today and you will see a huge gap. People in some countries live long, comfortable lives, while people in others still struggle to pay for food and medicine.
The gap has not always looked like this. About a thousand years ago, some of the world's most advanced cities stood in China, India and the Middle East, not in Europe.

Historians and economists give three kinds of answer: where a country is, how it is ruled, and what happened by chance. No single answer explains everything, and experts still argue about how much each one matters.
For most of human history, people lived in small groups that moved from place to place. They hunted animals and gathered wild plants, and they owned only what they could carry.
The last ice age ended about twelve thousand years ago. The climate became warmer and steadier, and this gave some groups of people a chance to try something new.
Over the next few thousand years, people in several parts of the world began to farm. They did it separately, because these places were far apart and knew nothing of each other.
In the hills and valleys of western Asia, wild wheat, barley, peas and lentils grew naturally. These plants were easy to gather, store and plant, so the people there had a very good start.
In China, people along the Yangtze river learned to grow rice, while farmers in the drier north grew millet. These crops fed very large numbers of people for thousands of years.
In Mexico, farmers slowly changed a wild grass into maize, which we also call corn. They grew it with beans and squash, and in the Andes people grew potatoes.
Farming also began on its own in parts of Africa and in New Guinea. Each place used the plants it had, such as sorghum in Africa and taro in New Guinea.
A farm can feed many more people than the same land can feed hunters. Farmers stayed in one place, built villages, and stored grain for the days when the harvest was poor.
Most wild plants are not worth farming, because they are poisonous, tiny or hard to grow. Places with a few really good plants had a head start over places without them.
In western Asia, people also tamed sheep, goats, cattle and pigs. These animals gave them meat, milk and wool, so a family could eat and dress from one small herd.
Oxen, and later horses, could pull a plough or a cart. One farmer could now grow more food than before, and goods could travel farther.
In the Americas, there were far fewer animals that people could tame. The llama could carry loads in the Andes, but it could not pull a plough or carry a rider far.
When people live close to animals, germs can jump from the animals to the people. Many illnesses, such as flu, began this way, and farming peoples slowly built up some protection against them.
When farmers made extra food, not everyone had to farm. Some people became potters, builders, priests or soldiers, and their work made life richer for everybody.
More than five thousand years ago, a city called Uruk grew up between two rivers in Mesopotamia. It had temples, walls and thousands of people, and few places like it had existed before.

The first writing was used to keep accounts, not to tell stories. Scribes in Mesopotamia pressed marks into wet clay to record grain and workers, and later people in other places invented writing too.
Rich farmland could support powerful rulers. They collected taxes, made laws, built roads and raised armies, and the biggest states could organise thousands of people at once.
People learned to melt copper and mix it with tin to make bronze, a hard metal. Later they learned to work iron, and this gave farmers better tools and soldiers better weapons.

Across the huge land of Eurasia, crops, tools and ideas travelled with traders. Wheat spread from western Asia to Europe and India, and paper, invented in China, slowly reached the Middle East and Europe.
Moving heavy goods by water is much cheaper than moving them over land. The Mediterranean Sea linked many peoples, and its harbours grew rich on trade.
Gunpowder, the compass and printing all began in China. They reached Europe over time, and printers, sailors and gunmakers there soon found new ways to use them.

Around the year 1500, Europe was split into many small states that competed with one another. Some historians think this helped, because a good idea banned in one place could still be tried in another.
In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed west from Spain and reached the Caribbean. Six years later, Vasco da Gama sailed around Africa and reached India for Portugal.
Europeans carried diseases such as smallpox and measles to the Americas, where nobody had resistance to them. Millions of people died, and historians still debate exactly how many.
Spanish and Portuguese colonies in the Americas sent silver and sugar to Europe. These goods made some merchants and kings very rich, and they paid for more ships and wars.

Over more than three centuries, over ten million Africans were forced onto ships and sold as slaves in the Americas. Historians still argue about how much this trade added to the wealth of Europe, but the suffering it caused was enormous.
In the 1700s, Britain had large amounts of coal close to the surface and close to its rivers and ports. Coal gave heat and power, and this helped to start the Industrial Revolution.
In 1712, Thomas Newcomen built a steam engine to pump water out of a coal mine. Later, James Watt made a much better engine, and steam power soon moved far beyond mines.

In the new mills of northern England, machines spun and wove cotton much faster than hands could. Cheap cloth was sold all over the world, although much of the raw cotton was grown by enslaved workers.

Why did the Industrial Revolution begin in Britain and not somewhere else? Historians suggest coal, high wages that made machines worth buying, busy trade and a lively interest in science, and they still argue about which mattered most.
People work and invest more when they are sure they can keep what they earn. Courts that enforce contracts and laws that protect property give them that confidence.

After 1688, the British Parliament held real power over the king, and it could not easily be ignored. Some scholars think this made investors feel safer, although it was only one part of a larger story.
In 1825, the world's first public steam railway opened in northern England. Within a few decades, rails crossed Europe and North America, and moving goods became much cheaper and faster.
Industry soon spread from Britain to Belgium, France, Germany and the United States. These countries did not have to invent everything, because they could copy British machines and improve them.
Countries that taught many children to read and count had workers who could use new machines. Some also built strong universities, where scientists and engineers learned their skills.
In 1796, Edward Jenner showed that a cowpox vaccine could protect people from smallpox. Later, clean water and sewers made cities healthier, and healthy people can work, learn and save for longer.

For most of history, ordinary people were about as poor as their grandparents had been. After about 1800, incomes began to rise fast in a few countries, and the gap between rich and poor lands opened wide.
After 1868, Japan sent students abroad, hired foreign experts and built railways and factories. It copied the best ideas of other countries and became an industrial nation within a few decades.

From the 1960s, South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore grew very fast by making goods for the world. After 1978, China also opened its economy, and hundreds of millions of its people escaped extreme poverty.
Geography still matters today. A country with no coast must send its goods through its neighbours, and a country with a lot of malaria loses workers and school days.
Many countries in Africa and Asia were ruled by European powers until the 1950s and 1960s. Their railways and ports were often built to carry raw materials out, not to link their own towns.
War destroys homes, farms, factories and lives. Countries that enjoy long periods of peace can save, build and trade, while countries at war must spend their wealth on fighting.
Chance has played a part, too, and the Black Death of the 1340s is a good example. It killed perhaps a third of the people of Europe, and the workers who survived could demand higher wages.
One idea has been tested again and again and found completely false. The differences in wealth between countries have nothing to do with how clever or capable their people are.

Most economists agree that some things help a country grow: peace, good health, schools, honest courts and trade with others. No country has a perfect recipe, and what works in one place may fail in another.
Put the three kinds of answer together and a fuller picture appears. Place gave some people a head start, rules decided how well they used it, and chance changed the story many times.
The list of rich countries has changed many times, and it will change again. A poor country today may be a rich one in a few generations, if the conditions are right.
C1C2: If you could look down at the Earth at night, you would see a strange pattern: some lands blaze with electric light, while others lie almost dark. Behind that pattern are very different lives, in which one person may expect comfort, good health and a long old age, and another a daily struggle to survive. This book asks the oldest question in economics, which is why the world ended up so uneven.

The present order is not ancient, and it is certainly not permanent. A thousand years ago, great cities such as Baghdad in the Middle East, Cairo in Egypt and Kaifeng in China were larger and more learned than almost anything in northern Europe. Anyone who had tried to predict then which region would grow richest would very probably have guessed wrong.

Scholars tend to offer three families of explanation: the geography a society was given, the rules and institutions it built for itself, and the sheer chance of events that nobody planned. Hardly anyone now believes that one of these alone can account for the whole story. The honest picture is a tangle of causes, and part of the interest lies in how they pulled on one another.

For hundreds of thousands of years, people lived in small bands that followed the seasons, hunting animals, fishing, and gathering wild plants, nuts and roots. Such a life was not necessarily miserable, but it left little room for building up wealth, since anything heavy had to be carried on the next move. Nobody could grow truly rich when everything they owned had to fit on their back.

Around twelve thousand years ago the last ice age drew to a close, and the glaciers retreated from large parts of the Northern Hemisphere. The climate that followed was warmer, wetter and, above all, far steadier than it had been for a very long time. That stability was the quiet background to one of the greatest changes in human history.

Over the following few thousand years, people in several regions of the world, quite independently of one another, began to plant seeds and tend animals instead of simply searching for them. It was a slow experiment rather than a sudden invention, and it must have involved countless failures. Yet it altered the human story more than any battle or any king ever has.

In the arc of land known as the Fertile Crescent, which curves from the Levant through southern Turkey into Mesopotamia, wild wheat, barley, peas and lentils grew in abundance. Their seeds were large, nourishing and easy to store, which made them ideal candidates for early farmers. Not every region of the world was handed such a helpful set of plants.

In China, rice was first grown in the wet lowlands near the Yangtze river, while farmers in the drier north turned to millet. Rice in particular could feed a great many people from a small patch of flooded field. It would become the food that supported some of the largest populations on Earth.

In what is now Mexico, farmers patiently reshaped a wild grass called teosinte until it became maize, with fat cobs that could feed a family through the winter. They planted it alongside beans and squash, which together made a surprisingly balanced diet. Far to the south, in the high Andes, other farmers were learning to grow potatoes in thin mountain soil.

Elsewhere, farming appeared in parts of Africa, where people grew sorghum and millet, and in the highlands of New Guinea, where they cultivated taro and bananas. Each region worked with whatever its own wild plants allowed, and the results were never quite equal. That inequality in the starting hand is where our story really begins.

A field of grain can feed far more people than the same land can feed hunters, and so farming societies grew quickly in number. Families settled in villages, built granaries, and learned to store food against the lean months. For the first time, a community could hold a surplus, and a surplus is the seed from which almost everything else in this story grows.

Most wild plants make poor crops, for they are bitter, tiny, slow to grow or simply not very nourishing. Regions that happened to hold a handful of excellent ones, such as large-seeded grasses, gave their farmers an early advantage. Some scholars think this small accident of botany shaped much of later history, though others say its importance has been exaggerated.

In western Asia, farmers also tamed wild sheep, goats, cattle and pigs, and then began to breed them for the qualities they found useful. These animals gave meat, milk, leather and wool, and a living herd could be kept alive until the day it was needed. Such creatures were stores of wealth that walked about on four legs.

Large animals offered something even more valuable than meat, and that was muscle. An ox could pull a plough through heavy soil that a person could not turn alone, and in time horses and donkeys carried loads and riders over distances that had once taken weeks on foot. Strength of this kind turned farms into engines of growth.

The Americas offered a very different set of animals, and few of them were suited to the farmyard. The llama of the Andes could carry a light load and give wool, yet it could not pull a plough or carry a rider far. This is one reason why farm work in the early Americas depended so much on human muscle.

Living in crowded villages beside herds and flocks gave germs a ready path from animals to people. Many diseases that later swept the world, including influenza, are thought to have begun this way, and communities that had lived with them for centuries built up some resistance. That resistance would later prove deadly to others, who had never met such illnesses at all.

Once farmers produced more than they needed, a share of the population was released from the fields to become potters, weavers, builders, priests, soldiers and scribes. Specialists practise their skills every day, and so they improve them far faster than anyone who does a little of everything. Towns grew up around these skilled workers, and some of the towns became the first cities.

More than five thousand years ago, in the flat river country of Mesopotamia, a city called Uruk grew behind great walls and around towering temples. Its people lived by irrigated farming, craftwork and trade, and they were governed by priests and rulers who organised the labour of thousands. It was among the earliest places in the world where strangers lived side by side in large numbers.

Writing began, so far as we can tell, as a form of bookkeeping: scribes in Mesopotamia pressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay to record grain, animals and workers. Records allowed rulers to collect taxes, settle disputes and plan far ahead, and so they made large governments possible. Writing was invented independently in at least two other places, China and Mesoamerica, though not in every region.

Wherever farming produced a steady surplus, rulers appeared to claim a share of it. They collected taxes, issued laws, fed their soldiers and built roads and canals, and the largest states learned to organise tens of thousands of people at a time. Such organisation could build an irrigation system or crush a rival, and it gave big states a lasting edge over small ones.

About five thousand years ago, metalworkers learned to mix copper with tin and make bronze, which is harder than copper and holds an edge far better than stone. Later came iron, which was cheaper because its ore is found almost everywhere. Iron tools and weapons spread widely, and states that could produce them in quantity gained both stronger farms and stronger armies.

Eurasia is a vast landmass, and across it crops, tools and ideas moved with merchants, soldiers and pilgrims over many centuries. Wheat travelled from western Asia to Europe and India, while paper, which the Chinese invented, found its way west to the Islamic world and eventually to Europe. A good idea that appeared in one place had a fair chance of reaching many others.

Before railways and lorries, a ship could carry a heavy cargo far more cheaply than a cart could carry it over land. Places with sheltered harbours and navigable rivers therefore had a natural advantage in trade, and the Mediterranean, ringed by busy ports, was the busiest of all trading seas. Coastlines mattered, and so did rivers that were deep enough to sail.

Gunpowder, the magnetic compass and printing all appeared first in China, and each of them travelled west along the trade routes. Europeans did not invent the first versions, but they adopted them eagerly and improved them, and the printing press that Johannes Gutenberg built in about 1450 spread books faster than any scribe could. History often rewards people who borrow well and improve on what they have borrowed.

Unlike China, which in 1500 was ruled by a single emperor, Europe was divided into many kingdoms, cities and duchies that were forever competing. Some historians argue that this rivalry was useful, because a thinker or merchant turned away by one ruler could simply try another. Others reply that the same quarrels also brought endless war, so the question is far from settled.

In 1492 Christopher Columbus, sailing for Spain, crossed the Atlantic and landed in the Caribbean, a part of the world that Europeans had not known. Six years later, Vasco da Gama of Portugal rounded the southern tip of Africa and reached the coast of India. Within a single decade, European ships had opened sea routes that connected the world's oceans for good.

The newcomers brought with them smallpox, measles and other diseases that had never before been known in the Americas, and the people there had no inherited resistance to them. Epidemics swept through towns and valleys, killing millions of people, though historians still disagree about the exact numbers. The collapse of these societies made it far easier for small groups of invaders to take control.

Mines in the Americas poured out silver, and plantations there grew sugar, tobacco and later cotton for markets across the Atlantic. The profits enriched merchants, kings and banks in Europe, and they paid for new ships, armies and trading companies. A world economy was taking shape, and its centre of gravity was slowly shifting towards the Atlantic coast.

Between the early 1500s and the 1860s, more than ten million Africans were seized, packed into ships and sold into slavery in the Americas. Historians still argue about how much this trade and the plantation economy added to the wealth of Britain and other European countries, but nobody doubts the scale of the suffering or the damage done to the societies the captives were taken from. Wealth for some countries was built in part on the misery of others.

In the eighteenth century, Britain was blessed with large deposits of coal, often lying near the surface and close to rivers and ports where it could be moved cheaply. Coal offered far more heat than wood, and it was the fuel that would drive the Industrial Revolution. Not every country had such fuel so conveniently to hand, and that mattered a great deal.

In 1712, an English ironmonger named Thomas Newcomen built a steam engine to pump floodwater out of a deep mine, and it was a clumsy machine that burned great quantities of coal. Half a century later, the Scottish engineer James Watt redesigned it to use far less fuel, and it became practical for workshops everywhere. For the first time in history, people had a machine that turned burning fuel into steady, tireless work.

In the mills of northern England, new machines spun and wove cotton thread at a speed that no hand-worker could match, and the cheap cloth they made was sold across the world. Much of the raw cotton, however, came from plantations in the American South, where it was grown and picked by enslaved people. The new factories, then, were joined to the old cruelty by long threads of trade.

Why did this change begin in Britain, and not in China, India or France, which were all large and skilful? Some historians point to its coal; others to high wages, which made it worth paying for machines that saved labour; and others to its trade, its lively interest in science and its habit of tinkering. The truth is probably a mixture, and each new generation of researchers weighs the ingredients differently.

Economists have long argued that rules matter as much as resources, because people will build, invest and take risks only when they are confident that they can keep the rewards. Fair courts, reliable contracts and protected property give them that confidence. Where a ruler or a powerful clique can seize whatever it likes, ambition tends to hide itself or move away.

In 1688 the English Parliament pushed out one king and invited another to rule, on the understanding that Parliament would hold real power over taxes and the law. Some scholars believe this made investors feel safer, since a king could no longer simply take their money. Even so, it was only one part of a much larger picture, and many other countries with strong rulers also grew rich later.

The first public railway to use steam locomotives opened in northern England in 1825, and within a few decades iron rails were spreading across Europe and North America. Farmers could reach distant markets, factories could receive coal and cotton on time, and cities could be fed from far away. A country with good railways could act like a single great market.

Within a few generations, industry had spread from Britain to Belgium, France, Germany and the United States, as engineers, skilled workers and machines crossed borders. Latecomers enjoyed one great advantage: they did not have to invent everything, because they could copy what already worked and avoid the old mistakes. Being second can be an excellent way to catch up.

A modern economy demands people who can read instructions, do sums and learn new skills, and countries that built schools early gained a lasting advantage. Some, such as Germany, also created strong universities and technical colleges, where chemists and engineers were trained in large numbers. Education turned out to be one of the best long-term investments that any nation could make.

In 1796 an English doctor, Edward Jenner, showed that a mild disease of cows could protect people against smallpox, and the idea of vaccination was born. In the century that followed, clean water, sewers and better food made cities far healthier places. Healthy people can work, learn and save for many more years, and so good health and rising wealth tend to feed each other.

For thousands of years, the average person earned barely more than their ancestors had, and a good harvest was usually followed by a rise in the number of mouths. Around 1800, in a few countries, incomes began to climb year after year, and the climb has never fully stopped. Historians call the widening gap between those countries and the rest the Great Divergence.

In 1868 a new government in Japan set out to catch up with the West, sending students abroad, hiring foreign experts and building railways, schools and factories at remarkable speed. Japan avoided being colonised by any European power, and within a few decades it had become an industrial nation and a military power. Its example showed that the pattern of rich and poor was not fixed.

From the 1960s, South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore grew at astonishing speed by educating their people and selling manufactured goods to the whole world. After 1978, China opened its own economy step by step, and since then several hundred million of its people have risen out of extreme poverty. These stories show that a country far behind can sometimes catch up within a lifetime.

Geography has not stopped mattering, even in the age of aircraft and the internet. A landlocked country must send its goods through the territory of its neighbours, which raises the cost of trade, and illnesses such as malaria drain the strength of workers and the school attendance of children. Yet geography is a handicap rather than a sentence, since Switzerland has no coast and Singapore has hardly any natural resources.

For long periods, much of Africa, Asia and the Caribbean was ruled from Europe, and the borders drawn by outsiders often cut across older homelands. Colonial ports and railways were frequently designed to carry raw materials to the coast and onto ships, rather than to link the colony's own towns and markets. Many countries became independent only in the 1950s and 1960s, and they started that new life with few schools and fewer factories.

War destroys homes, harvests and factories, and it also destroys trust, which is slower to rebuild than any bridge. A country that enjoys decades of peace can save, invest and trade with its neighbours, while one that is repeatedly at war must spend its resources on survival. Some of the poorest places in the world today are those that have suffered the longest conflicts.

Chance has also played its part, and few accidents were as large as the Black Death, which reached Europe in 1347 and killed perhaps a third of its people. Workers became so scarce that many could demand higher wages, and some historians think this weakened the old system of landlords and serfs. Others warn that the effects varied greatly from place to place, so the plague should be treated as one possible ingredient rather than a master key.

One explanation can be set aside firmly, because it has been tested many times and found false: the notion that some peoples are born cleverer or more capable than others. Human beings everywhere are equally able, and the same peoples who were poor in one century have been rich in another. What differs is the setting they were given, the rules they live under and the accidents that have shaped them.

Most economists would agree that a handful of ingredients help any country to prosper: peace, public health, schooling, honest courts and open trade with the world. None of them is a magic switch, however, and a policy that succeeds in one setting can fail miserably in another. Wealth, in the end, seems to come from many small things working together for a long time.

When the three strands of explanation are woven together, a fuller and more honest picture begins to appear. Place gave certain societies a head start in crops, animals and trade; rules and institutions decided how well they used that start; and chance, in the form of plagues, wars and lucky discoveries, kept rearranging the board. No single cause was enough by itself, and that is exactly why the question has lasted so long.

The league table of wealthy nations has been reshuffled many times, and it will certainly be reshuffled again. Poor countries are not condemned by their geography or their past, and a few of them have shown that the gap can be crossed within a lifetime. The question of why some countries got rich first is old, but the more useful question for our own time may be how many more can follow.
